title: Why catching a rocket matters - and what it does not prove
dek: SpaceX's tower caught a Starship returning from orbit. To see why that is a big deal, start with an aeroplane ticket.

statements.why: Like aeroplanes, hardware that flies again does not have to be rebuilt each time.

statements.why: NASA plans to use a version of Starship as its Moon lander.

article: When SpaceX's giant tower arms closed around a returning Starship on 14 November, the company celebrated a first. But what does the milestone actually mean - and what does it not mean?

To understand why a catch matters, think about air travel. Imagine if every passenger jet were scrapped after a single flight: tickets would be unaffordable. For most of the space age, rockets worked exactly like that, and each launch threw away hardware worth tens of millions of dollars.

SpaceX began to change this about a decade ago by landing and reusing the first stage of its Falcon 9 rocket. Analysts estimate this helped bring the cost of putting a kilogram into orbit down to roughly $2,700, compared with $10,000 or more in the era of throwaway rockets. Yet Falcon 9's upper stage is still discarded on every flight.

Starship is designed to go further: both of its stages are meant to return and fly again quickly. If that works, supporters believe launch costs could fall to somewhere between $10 and $50 a kilogram. Catching the upper stage, which faces the fiercest heat as it plunges back through the atmosphere, is an essential step towards that goal.

Cheaper, more frequent launches would ripple outwards. Starship can carry far more of SpaceX's newest Starlink internet satellites, each of which handles about ten times the traffic of the previous model. Elon Musk has said SpaceX will retire Falcon 9 once Starship flies reliably every week.

The milestone also matters for the Moon. NASA plans to use a version of Starship to land astronauts there, but the lander must be refuelled in orbit, by some estimates with around ten tanker flights. That plan only makes sense if launches become routine and affordable.

Nevertheless, caution is warranted. The $10-to-$50 figure is a target, not an established price, and some analysts point out that Musk's numbers describe SpaceX's own costs rather than what customers will pay. On the same flight, the booster was lost, and no Ship has yet been inspected, refuelled and relaunched quickly - the real test of reuse.
In short, the catch shows that the hardest piece of the puzzle can come home intact. Whether it can turn into cheap, airline-style spaceflight is a question the next few years will answer.

glossary.def: an important event that marks progress
thrown away because it is no longer wanted
too expensive for people to pay for
experts who study information and explain it
spread its effects more and more widely
stop using something because it is old or replaced
reasonable or justified in the situation

tasks.q: Which sentence best sums up the WHOLE article?
options: Catching Starship is a key step towards cheap, reusable spaceflight, but it does not prove that yet
SpaceX has now made spaceflight as cheap as air travel
SpaceX will stop using Falcon 9 next year
SpaceX's newest Starlink satellites carry ten times more traffic
tasks.explain: A matches the question in paragraph 1 and the answer in paragraph 8. B is an overclaim (paragraph 7 says the costs are only targets). C twists paragraph 5: Falcon 9 retires only once Starship flies weekly. D is one detail from paragraph 5.

tasks.q: Put the history of rocket reuse in order (paragraphs 2-4).
items: Rockets are thrown away after every launch
Falcon 9 lands and reuses its first stage
A Starship upper stage is caught by the tower
Both stages return and fly again quickly (the goal)
tasks.explain: Signal words help: "For most of the space age" (past), "about a decade ago" (Falcon 9), "on 14 November" (the catch), and "is designed to" / "goal" (the future).

tasks.q: Scan the article: what does each figure refer to?

pairs.right: cost per kilogram in the throwaway-rocket era
hoped-for cost per kilogram with Starship
the day the Ship was caught

tasks.explain: The three money figures tell a story of falling costs. Notice the last one is a hope, not a fact (paragraph 7).

statements.text: Falcon 9's upper stage is reused on every flight.
statements.explain: Paragraph 3: it "is still discarded on every flight".

statements.text: The upper stage faces extreme heat when it comes back through the atmosphere.
statements.explain: Paragraph 4: it "faces the fiercest heat as it plunges back through the atmosphere".

statements.text: Starship will take passengers to Mars within five years.
statements.explain: Mars is never mentioned in the article.

statements.text: Some analysts say Musk's figures describe SpaceX's own costs, not customer prices.
statements.explain: Paragraph 7 says exactly this, in slightly different words.

statements.text: NASA has fixed a date for the Starship Moon landing.
statements.explain: Paragraph 6 explains NASA's plan but gives no date at all.

tasks.q: From paragraph 6, what can we infer about refuelling the Moon lander with many tanker flights?
options: It would be far too costly unless launches become cheap and frequent
It has already been tested successfully many times
It is no longer part of NASA's plan
It will be done by Falcon 9 rockets
tasks.explain: "That plan only makes sense if launches become routine and affordable" - so without cheap, frequent launches, ten tanker flights would be impractical. B, C and D are not supported.

tasks.q: In paragraph 7, "caution is warranted" is closest in meaning to:
options: it is reasonable to be careful
there is nothing to worry about
tasks.explain: "Nevertheless" signals a turn, and the rest of the paragraph lists reasons to be careful. So caution is justified - "warranted".

tasks.q: Why does the writer compare rockets to passenger jets in paragraph 2?
options: To explain why throwing rockets away makes launches so expensive
To argue that rockets are safer than aeroplanes
To suggest that SpaceX should start an airline
To show that aeroplane tickets are becoming more expensive
tasks.explain: The analogy makes an unfamiliar idea familiar: scrapping a jet after one flight would make tickets unaffordable, and that is how rockets used to work.

write.prompt: Do you think reusable rockets will make space travel common in your lifetime? Write 2-3 sentences in English, using one word from today's list.
write.sample: I think reusable rockets could make space travel more routine, but I am not sure it will happen soon. The catch was an important milestone, yet caution is warranted until a Ship actually flies again.
